hardware: Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz (stated only in linked issue #47 title/body, not in the table)
name: TurboPFor Integer Compression
workload: icapp benchmark on 100M Zipfian integers (block 128/256) and the gov2.sorted docid set, single thread, encode and decode MB/s
claimed_speedup: ZIPF table: TurboPack scalar 11694 MB/s encode / 8876 decode vs Simple-8b 848 / 3832; TurboPackV sse 17357 / 12363; TurboVByte 11191 / 10333 vs FP_VByte 5200 / 4268. Ratios (derived from page data): TurboPackV decode ~3.2x Simple-8b, TurboVByte decode ~2.4x FP_VByte. Compression ratio of TurboPack equals fixed-width packing (25.0%) and Simple-8b is 24.0%, so Simple-8b packs slightly smaller there.
stars_or_usage: 848 stars; used by Debian Code Search
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0 (commercial license offered by author), so copyleft; C library with C++ headers; SSE/AVX2/NEON/Power9 paths; direct access to bit-packed entries without decompression; no input validation promised beyond 'normally does not read outside buffers'.
caveats: Numbers come from the TurboPFor README, written by the author of a competing library (TurboPFor); README table gives no CPU or flags (the README links an issue titled 'Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz gcc 9.2' whose page lists the CPU but no compiler flags), and the table is labelled 2019.11. Compiler flags unstated, so not tier A. Self-reported 'No other Integer Compression compress/decompress faster' is marketing wording. FastPFor rows use partly 64Ki blocks marked with (*).
found_via: WebSearch: 'C++ SIMD integer compression bit packing faster than FastPFor varint github'; then opened the repo README

name: FastPFor (FastPFOR C++ library)
baseline: Simple-8b and VByte (as measured in the TurboPFor README table)
workload: Same TurboPFor icapp ZIPF benchmark (100M Zipfian integers): FP_SimdFastPFor 64Ki block decode vs Simple-8b and FP_VByte
claimed_speedup: Repo README: 'can decode at least 4 billions of compressed integers per second ... 15 GB/s', 'significantly faster than generic codecs like gzip, LZO, Snappy or LZ4'. Third-party table (TurboPFor README, ZIPF): FP_SimdFastPFor 8748 MB/s decode vs Simple-8b 3832 (~2.3x, derived from page data) and vs FP_VByte 4268 (~2.0x, derived from page data); encode 624 MB/s is slower than Simple-8b 848.
stars_or_usage: 978 stars; DuckDB derived code from it; Lucene 4.6 PForDelta format derived from FastPFOR
tradeoffs: Research library for 32-bit integers (64-bit coverage is partial); SSSE3 minimum for key codecs, NEON on aarch64; no input validation during decode (documented); best codecs need 128-integer or larger blocks (FastPFor itself needs larger blocks than SIMD binary packing).
caveats: The repo README claims are against gzip/LZO/Snappy/LZ4 (not in the baseline list). The Simple-8b and VByte comparison is derived from a competitor's table that gives no flags; encode speed of SimdFastPFor is lower than Simple-8b in that table. The SPE 2015 paper 'Decoding billions of integers per second through vectorization' (peer reviewed, seen only as a WebSearch snippet because arXiv and Wiley were blocked) is the primary evidence and was not opened. Note FastPFor is itself the baseline other catalog entries beat.
found_via: WebSearch: 'C++ SIMD integer compression bit packing faster than FastPFor varint github'; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: simdcomp
workload: gov2.sorted docid set, block 128 with delta coding, single thread (TurboPFor README table row SC_SIMDPack128)
claimed_speedup: Third-party table: SC_SIMDPack128 6952 MB/s encode / 9488 MB/s decode vs Simple-8b 836 / 3296 and FP_Vbyte 1888 / 1980 (derived from page data: ~8.3x encode and ~2.9x decode vs Simple-8b; ~3.7x and ~4.8x vs FP_Vbyte). Compression ratio 21.8% vs Simple-8b 18.9%. Repo README: 'decode at least 4 billions of compressed integers per second' and '0.3 cycles per integer on a Skylake'.
stars_or_usage: 538 stars; used by upscaledb, EventQL, ManticoreSearch
tradeoffs: Binary packing of 128-integer blocks, so worse compression than Simple-8b / PFor on skewed data; needs SSE2/SSE4.1 or NEON; C API usable from C++; the 128-block unit is bad for short arrays (LittleIntPacker targets that).
caveats: Numbers come from the TurboPFor README, written by the author of a competing library (TurboPFor); README table gives no CPU or flags (the README links an issue titled 'Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz gcc 9.2' whose page lists the CPU but no compiler flags), and the table is labelled 2019.11. The repo's own bitpackingbenchmark reports cycles per integer but the README gives no baseline comparison; the 15 GB/s claim compares to gzip/LZO/Snappy/LZ4.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github lemire streamvbyte simdcomp SIMD-BP128 integer compression library'; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

hardware: Skylake i7-6700 (TurboPFor issue #47) for the competitor table; Apple M4 Max for the repo's own numbers
name: StreamVByte
baseline: VByte / varint (FP_VByte, PC_Vbyte) and Google Group Varint
workload: TurboPFor ZIPF (100M integers, 0..255 skew) and gov2.sorted; encode/decode MB/s, single thread, 'Streamvbyte 2019' row
claimed_speedup: Third-party table: ZIPF StreamVbyte 11197 MB/s encode / 11984 decode vs FP_VByte 5200 / 4268 (derived from page data: ~2.2x encode, ~2.8x decode); gov2 StreamVbyte 8456 / 9476 vs FP_Vbyte 1888 / 1980 (~4.5x, ~4.8x derived). Repo README: ~27 GB/s encode, ~41 GB/s decode (mixed 1-4 byte) on an Apple M4 Max, no baseline in that table.
stars_or_usage: 419 stars; used by RediSearch, StarRocks, Facebook Thrift, upscaledb, tilemaker
tradeoffs: Byte-aligned, so compression ratio is worse than bit-packing (31.2% on ZIPF vs 25.0% for TurboPack); decoder may read STREAMVBYTE_PADDING bytes past input; SSE4.1 / NEON with runtime dispatch and scalar fallback.
caveats: Numbers come from the TurboPFor README, written by the author of a competing library (TurboPFor); README table gives no CPU or flags (the README links an issue titled 'Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz gcc 9.2' whose page lists the CPU but no compiler flags), and the table is labelled 2019.11. Newer StreamVByte code (version 3.0.0, April 2026) differs from the '2019' build in the table. The competitor repo also claims TurboByte is faster than StreamVByte (issue #96, no CPU or flags stated).
found_via: WebSearch: 'github lemire streamvbyte simdcomp SIMD-BP128 integer compression library'; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: MaskedVByte
workload: TurboPFor ZIPF and gov2.sorted decode of VByte-compressed integers, single thread
claimed_speedup: Third-party table: ZIPF MaskedVByte 6689 MB/s encode / 9524 decode vs FP_VByte 5200 / 4268 and PC_Vbyte 2260 / 4208 (derived from page data: ~2.2x decode vs FP_VByte); gov2 MaskedVByte 2740 / 3384 vs FP_Vbyte 1888 / 1980 (~1.7x decode, ~1.5x encode derived).
stars_or_usage: 131 stars; integrated into Apache Lucene experiments and PISA
tradeoffs: Decodes the standard VByte format, so it is format-compatible with ordinary varint; needs SSE4.1 or NEON; 32-bit integers only.
caveats: Numbers come from the TurboPFor README, written by the author of a competing library (TurboPFor); README table gives no CPU or flags (the README links an issue titled 'Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz gcc 9.2' whose page lists the CPU but no compiler flags), and the table is labelled 2019.11. The repo README itself has no numbers; the paper (Plaisance, Kurz, Lemire, 'Vectorized VByte Decoding', 2015) is on arXiv, which was blocked, so it was not opened.
found_via: Listed in the FastPFor and TurboPFor READMEs; opened github.com/lemire/MaskedVByte

compiler_and_flags: Release build via CMake; compiler and flags not stated
name: SIMDCompressionAndIntersection
workload: vteromero shootout on gov2.sorted, delta-coded sorted 32-bit integer lists, i7-6700HQ; the library supplies the Delta+BinaryPacking, Delta+FastPFor and Delta+VariableByte codecs
claimed_speedup: Shootout row Delta+BinaryPacking 2.30 G/s encode / 2.33 G/s decode vs Delta+VariableByte 1.62 / 1.52 and Delta+FastPFor128 615.66 M/s (derived from page data: ~1.4x / ~1.5x vs VByte, ~3.7x vs FastPFor128). Repo README: 'decode at least 4 billions of compressed integers per second ... 15 GB/s'.
tradeoffs: C++11 library for sorted lists with SIMD differential coding plus SIMD set-intersection routines; SSE2 required, SSE4.1 for some codecs; pre-sorted input expected for the delta schemes.
caveats: The shootout's 'BinaryPacking' row may be the scalar variant rather than SIMDBinaryPacking (not confirmed); the shootout is by the author of a competing codec (VTEnc). The library overlaps with FastPFor and simdcomp code, which are listed separately. Compiler flags unstated.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/integer-compression?l=c%2B%2B; benchmark from vteromero/integer-compression-benchmarks

compiler_and_flags: Release CMake build; compiler and flags not stated
name: VTEnc
baseline: FastPFor, BinaryPacking, VariableByte, VarIntGB (sorted-list integer codecs)
workload: Sorted timestamp list ts.txt (text file of timestamps) and gov2.sorted, encode and decode speed and compression ratio on an i7-6700HQ
claimed_speedup: ts.txt: VTEnc/1 102.28 G/s encode, 7.32 G/s decode, ratio 26,622 vs Delta+FastPFor256 1.45 G/s / 3.61 G/s, ratio 489.4 and Delta+VariableByte 3.89 G/s / 3.43 G/s, ratio 4.0 (derived from page data: ~70x encode and ~2.0x decode vs FastPFor256). gov2.sorted: VTEnc/1 gives the best ratio (8.29) but decodes at 210.99 M/s, far slower than Delta+BinaryPacking 2.33 G/s.
tradeoffs: Cluster-based encoding for sorted integer sets, not a bit-packer; the repo warns the format may change dramatically between versions; encoder can be very slow on gov2.
caveats: Speed win holds only on the highly regular timestamp file; on gov2.sorted it is slower than all bit-packing and varint baselines but compresses best. The author runs the shootout. Compiler flags unstated. Tangential to bit-packing, kept because it is compared directly to FastPFor/BinaryPacking/VByte.
